newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spanish prices fall, unemployment rises.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spanish prices fall, unemployment rises.

text.p: Spanish inflation moderated and unemployment rose in September, but analysts said that while the figures gave the Bank of Spain greater scope for interest rate reductions it was unlikely to make any swift move.
Spain reported on Friday that consumer prices rose just 3.6 percent year-on-year in September, down from 3.7 percent in August, with an especially tame 0.2 percent month-on-month rise.
The jobless rate climbed to 13.82 percent last month from 13.5 percent in August.

Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato called the inflation news positive, but added that the unemployment rise stemmed from seasonal factors in the service sector that would continue to create problems throughout autumn and winter.
"The news on the price index was very positive," Rato told journalists at the swearing in of a new president of Spanish stock exchange watchdog CNMV.

"The increase in September unemployment is a consequence of the seasonality of service sector employment. We've got to maintain an optimistic attitude but certainly in the next period of autumn and winter employment related to services will fall," Rato said.

But despite flagging employment and tame inflation, economists said the Bank of Spain was unlikely to sanction another cut in its key money market rate again so soon, particularly given worries about rising wage costs.

At present, wages are rising at about a four percent pace, but the government's 1997 budget draft foresees a far more modest increase of 2.8 percent -- one more in line with its 1997 inflation target of 2.6 percent.
"It's one of the most important and probably the most important thing in keeping inflation pressures (under control) in the future," Rato said.
Last Thursday's Bank of Spain cut, the sixth this year, brought the rate down 50 basis points to 6.75 percent in recognition of the government's austere 1997 budget draft.

"I don't think (the data) changes the Bank of Spain's outlook since a decision of this type should be taken from a broader perspective and not from isolated numbers," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
In a separate statement, Spain's Economy Ministry said the inflation data showed prices were headed toward the government's 3.4 percent 1996 inflation goal.
"This puts us on the right path for complying with the inflation criteria set by the Maastricht Treaty," the statement said.

According to the terms of the Maastricht Treaty, countries which want to join in the common currency must meet strict economic goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public borrowing in 1997.
The minority Popular Party government has made clear that joining European monetary union in 1999 is one of its top goals and that its 1997 budget draft was a good step in that direction.
